mech: A swollen, land-hungry English gentry and nobility found in French wars an outlet for younger sons and a source of ransom and plunder.
Overpopulated France entered its crisis phase with a squeezed peasantry and an indebted nobility that split along factional lines once war came.
Defeat at Poitiers (1356), the king's capture and noble ransoms paid by peasants left the countryside taxed and unprotected.
The crisis phase of the cycle (1310-1400): falling rents, elite infighting and a state that could no longer pay its own defenders.
Plague killed perhaps 40 percent of the English, so labour became scarce and peasants resisted the Statute of Labourers that tried to freeze wages.
The same demographic shock only became revolt because English lords tried to re-impose servile dues and English villages were organised enough to fight back.
The rising failed militarily but showed lords that servile dues could not be enforced, and villeinage withered over the next century.
With land abundant and hands scarce, tenants could walk away to better terms and lords had to bargain.
East of the Elbe the same labour shortage strengthened lords, because weak village communities could not resist and grain export to the west paid for coercion.
A common shock hitting small initial differences in institutions sent western and eastern Europe down opposite paths.
In the depression phase, elite numbers outran shrinking rents; armed retinues and noble factions fought over royal patronage.
England's population about doubled from 1500 to 1640; prices rose faster than crown revenue, gentry multiplied and competed for office, and the state went broke.
The stagflation phase (1580-1640) produced elite overproduction and fiscal strain that made the crisis of 1640 likely.
Cold, wet harvests of the late 1630s and 1640s added hunger and plague to the political crisis of the three Stuart kingdoms.
Hobbes wrote Leviathan in Paris exile, during and against the civil war, to argue that any sovereign is better than war of all against all.
By 1560 France was as crowded as before the Black Death; noble numbers and debts grew, and religious faction gave elite rivalry a banner.
War taxation on a population that had recovered to its ceiling, plus office-holders defending their privileges, set Paris against the crown.
The harvest failure of 1647-48 doubled bread prices in Paris the year the barricades went up.
Conquest made a few senatorial families enormously rich while Italian smallholders lost their land; aspirants to office multiplied faster than offices.
Generals with personally loyal armies fought each other until one of them, Octavian, held all power.
After the Antonine peak the empire entered its stagflation and crisis phases: falling population, fiscal strain and usurpers.
The expansion phase of Muscovy ended under Ivan IV; a populous center, a swollen service nobility and the oprichnina left the state brittle.
Sulphate from the Peruvian eruption cooled the northern summer of 1601; frosts and rain destroyed Russian harvests three years running.
Famine killed a large part of the population, discredited Tsar Boris Godunov and fed the armies of the first False Dmitry.
The worst drought and cold of the Little Ice Age in Anatolia (1591-96) collided with Ottoman war demands for grain and men.
Anatolia's population grew fast in the sixteenth century; landless young men became mercenary musketeers, and price inflation broke the timar system.
Years of drought and locusts in Shaanxi and Henan turned unpaid soldiers and starving peasants into rebel armies.
A doubled population and a fixed land tax left the Ming unable to pay its armies; the dismissed postal and frontier soldiers joined the rebels.
A fall in Japanese and Spanish American silver reaching China in the late 1630s made taxes payable in silver harder to collect.
Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644 and the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself.
Thirty years of war with the Manchu state drained Ming silver into the northeast frontier armies; the Qing then took Beijing from Li Zicheng.
The coldest decades of the Little Ice Age shortened growing seasons across the hemisphere just as states were waging their most expensive wars.
Across 1400-1900, cold phases line up with falling harvests, more wars and population decline, in Europe and in China.
Population growth outran land and official posts; failed examination candidates, like the Taiping leader Hong Xiuquan, led the angry.
To beat the Taiping the court let provincial gentry raise their own armies and taxes, and power never fully returned to Beijing.
The generals raised to crush the Yellow Turbans, Cao Cao among them, kept their armies and split the empire.
After 763 the Tang ruled through semi-independent military governors; the court never again taxed the whole empire directly.
The rebel army took Chang'an in 756 and Emperor Xuanzong fled to Sichuan.
To survive invasion and usurpation the empire roughly doubled its army and bureaucracy and taxed land and heads to pay for them.
Each extra solidus spent on defence bought less security; peasants abandoned taxed land and the West could not afford its own survival.
A late Roman state run for a narrow senatorial and military elite pressed so hard on taxpayers that many had little reason to defend it.
Cariaco Basin and Yok Balum cave records show multiyear droughts around 810, 860 and 910 that match the waves of abandonment.
A drying trend after 660 coincides with a rise in recorded war events on Maya monuments.
Competing holy lords spent on monuments and war; in the Petexbatun the collapse came with fortifications and sieges before any drought.
Dense Late Classic populations farmed eroding hillsides near their limit, so dry years hit an already overstretched system run by too many nobles.
Royal dynasties of the southern lowlands stopped raising dated monuments; populations moved north or dispersed.
Tree rings from Vietnam show decades-long droughts broken by intense monsoons that silted and broke the hydraulic network Angkor lived on.
After the Ayutthaya attack, the court moved to the Mekong confluence where maritime trade, not rice tribute, paid for kingship.
Colder summers cut hay for cattle while the Norse kept a European farming identity and did not take up Inuit seal hunting.
Plague in Norway and a falling market for walrus ivory cut the shipping links a small, specialised colony depended on.
A severe drought from about 1130 hit a regional system that imported maize and timber into Chaco Canyon.
Droughts in the mid-1100s and later 1200s struck a maize-dependent city of perhaps ten to twenty thousand.
At Tell Leilan the dry-farming plains of the Khabur were abandoned as the drought began, cutting the grain base of Akkadian rule.
Low Nile floods are proposed to have undermined the grain economy of the late Old Kingdom.
A weakening monsoon dried the floodwater farming of the Indus plains; cities shrank and people moved east to wetter Ganges lands.
Diamond reads the killing partly as Malthusian: land-starved young men, and killings even among Hutu over land in one commune.
Belgian rule (Rwanda was administered alongside the Congo) turned Hutu and Tutsi into fixed racial identities on identity cards, which the 1959 revolution and Hutu Power politicised.
Top-down forest management reversed Japan's seventeenth-century timber crisis; Diamond uses it as a society that chose not to fail.
note: prevented: the deforestation crisis from becoming a collapse of the Tokugawa order

mech: Islanders felled palms for canoes, fuel, farms and the rollers and sledges that moved the moai.
Polynesian rats arriving with the settlers multiplied without predators and ate the palm nuts, so the forest could not regenerate.
On open, windswept ground, stone mulch kept soil moist and fertile enough for sweet potato.
Garden agriculture let a population of a few thousand live on a treeless island; Bayesian chronologies show monument building continued to contact.
note: prevented: deforestation from turning into a pre-contact demographic collapse

mech: Repeated visits brought venereal disease, smallpox and tuberculosis to a population with no prior exposure.
Raiders took perhaps half the population to Peru; the few repatriated brought smallpox, and missionaries moved many of the rest to Tahiti.

view: Historians of the Pacific labour trade
mech: Once charted, the island lay on Pacific shipping lanes used by whalers and, in 1862, by Peruvian labour recruiters.
Pollen and lake cores show a dry spell beginning before the destructions; letters from Ugarit and Hatti ask for grain.
Drought and famine around the Aegean and Anatolia set people moving by land and sea toward Egypt and the Levant.
Hittite kings begged Egypt and Ugarit for grain shipments; the capital was then abandoned and burned.
Ugarit's last letters report enemy ships burning its towns while its own fleet and troops were away in Hittite service.
Migrant raiders, recorded by Ramesses III, destroyed coastal cities from Anatolia to the Levant.
Barbarian infantry with javelins and long swords learned to beat the chariot armies the palace kingdoms relied on.
Crushed skeletons and tilted walls at Mycenae, Tiryns and Troy fit a sequence of large earthquakes.
Losing a hub like Ugarit broke the trade in copper, tin and grain that tied Egypt, Hatti, Cyprus and Mycenae together.
With its capital abandoned, the Hittite state dissolved into Neo-Hittite city kingdoms in Syria.
Every Mycenaean palace burned or was abandoned; Linear B writing ended with them.
Egypt survived the attacks but lost its Levantine empire and its trading partners; strikes, tomb robbery and division followed.
Without palaces to organise them, Greek communities lost writing and long-distance trade and shrank to villages.
Freed from Egyptian and Hittite overlords and with Ugarit gone, Tyre, Sidon and Byblos took over Mediterranean trade.
A merchant culture without palace scribes favoured a short alphabet over cuneiform and Linear B.
When tin routes broke, smiths in Cyprus and the Levant turned to local iron ore, which needed no long-distance trade.
The fall of the palaces destroyed the wealth of the palace elite: Dark Age graves and houses are far more equal than Mycenaean ones.

view: Joseph McConnell, Andrew Wilson and colleagues
mech: Lead emissions in Greenland ice drop abruptly with the plague of 165 and stay low for five centuries: miners died and mines closed.
The first pandemic killed perhaps 10 to 20 percent of the empire and ended the Roman demographic and fiscal boom.
A second pandemic in the 250s struck an empire already at war on two fronts, and the frontier and the coinage gave way together.
With little new silver mined, the mint recycled old coin and stretched it with copper; the lead minimum matches the final debasement.
Emperors paid soldiers in ever more coins of ever less silver, a hidden tax that prices eventually exposed.
With money nearly worthless, Diocletian moved taxes into kind and fixed prices by edict in 301.
Goths fleeing the Huns were admitted, then starved and abused by Roman officials, rebelled and destroyed an eastern field army.
A Gothic army now lived permanently inside the empire; under Alaric it extracted payments and finally took Rome.
Loss of Africa's taxes to the Vandals (439) after the Goths and others carved up Gaul and Spain left the West too poor to pay an army.
When the state and its army stopped paying, the specialised economy of the West fell apart: fewer cattle, worse pottery, no coins.
The end of the Roman tax system mattered most: aristocrats got poorer and peasants, less taxed, often got freer.
Senatorial fortunes spread across provinces could not survive the end of the empire that guarded them; inequality fell with everything else.
The volcanic cold of 536-540 may have shifted rodent and flea ecology just before plague reached Egypt in 541.
A century of cold weakened the agrarian empires of Rome and Persia while Arabia, they argue, grew greener and more mobile.
Recurring plague waves thinned the taxpayers and soldiers of both empires before the Arab conquests.
The Masmuda of the High Atlas, fused by the Mahdi Ibn Tumart's reform preaching, overran a Sanhaja dynasty softened by city life in Marrakesh.
Zenata nomads of the steppe fringe took Fez and then Marrakesh as Almohad cohesion dissolved into court intrigue.
Ibn Khaldun names Qadisiyya and Yarmuk: a new faith erased rivalry among tribes, so some thirty thousand Arabs beat a far larger Persian army.
The same cohesion carried the Arab armies against the Roman field army of Heraclius in Syria.
Defeat in Iraq opened the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon; the last shah died in flight in 651.
Hulegu's army, drawn from steppe peoples welded together by Chinggis Khan, stormed Baghdad and killed the caliph.
The fall of the city ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad.
The Xiongnu confederacy formed as China unified, because only a unified steppe could extort trade and gifts from a unified China.
Empires on either side of the agro-pastoral frontier scaled up in tandem: across two millennia most megaempires sit on that frontier.
A simulation seeded only with the spread of mounted warfare from the steppe reproduces where and when large states arose in the Old World.
Mounted archers gave the steppe its military edge; the model puts the most intense warfare on the steppe frontier.
Two centuries on the frontier with the steppe khanates forged Muscovite cohesion; throwing off Tatar overlordship launched expansion.
A frontier principality of holy warriors against Byzantium drew fighters with the ideal of ghaza and grew by conquest.
The early Ottomans were a plunder confederacy that welcomed Christian lords and soldiers; cohesion came from shared booty more than faith.
The Fulani jihad's reform cohesion turned Oyo's northern garrison town Ilorin into an emirate, and Ilorin's cavalry broke Oyo.

view: Victoria Tin-bor Hui (war made the state)
mech: Two centuries of total war rewarded the state that mobilised hardest; Qin conscripted, registered and rewarded every household.
Shang Yang's reforms built the first impersonal, merit-based bureaucratic state, two thousand years before Europe.
Seventeenth-century wars pushed European rulers to bargain with capital-holders for credit, building the fiscal-military state.
Parliamentary control of taxes made the crown a credible borrower; interest rates fell and public debt soared.
Britain met the 'doorstep conditions' (rule of law for elites, perpetual organisations, political control of the army) and later opened access to all.
With no dynasty, the New Army commanders ruled provinces as private domains.
Comfortable housing for most residents looks like a city that turned away from god-kings and monument-building toward collective welfare.
note: prevented: one-man rule (a reading of the evidence, not a recorded event)

mech: Rich ore and too few willing workers led Toledo to conscript highland villages for the mines.
Mercury amalgamation made low-grade ore worth mining at scale, multiplying the demand for labour.
Comparing villages on either side of the mita boundary: haciendas avoided mita lands, so mita districts got fewer roads and less land security.
Same people, culture and geography; different institutions on either side of a line drawn in 1945.
South Korea grew under dictators by investing in schooling and following growth policies; democracy and secure institutions came after the growth.
The Soviet zone became the Democratic People's Republic in 1948.
State farms and a public distribution system starved the regions the regime cared least about when output fell.
The end of Soviet subsidised oil and fertiliser cut North Korean grain output just before the floods of 1995.
Closing the council let established merchant families lock newcomers out of the long-distance trade contracts that had made Venice rich.
Pluralist institutions after 1688 protected property and opened markets, so inventors and entrepreneurs could profit from innovation.
American land (sugar, cotton, timber) and accessible coal freed Britain from the land constraint that also bound the Yangzi delta.
What changed was talk: a new dignity and liberty for ordinary commerce and innovation, first in Holland and Britain.
Only in Britain were wages high and coal cheap enough to make labour-saving coal-burning machines pay; that is why they were invented there.
Egypt's absentee Mamluk landlords kept squeezing rent after the plague and let irrigation decay, so Egypt never recovered as England did.
Rival claimants after the defeat at Mbwila (1665) financed civil war by selling captives, and the kingdom split into warring factions.
Across Africa, regions that exported more slaves are poorer and have weaker states today; raiding set neighbours and kin against each other.
Overtaxed peasants fled or rebelled and nobles fought for scarce assignments, so the centre lost its grip.
Nader Shah's victory at Karnal opened Delhi; his army sacked it and carried off the Peacock Throne.
The sack showed the emperor could not defend his capital; provincial dynasties stopped remitting revenue.
Mass death made labour scarce and land abundant: real wages rose and the share of the rich fell, in Europe and in Mamluk Egypt alike.
Italian tax records show inequality falling after 1348; but later plagues, such as 1630, did not level, because inheritance law had changed.
War labour boards, high demand for less-skilled workers and a flood of educated workers compressed the US wage structure in the 1940s.
Mass-mobilisation war destroyed capital, brought confiscatory top tax rates and controls, and cut top income shares across the belligerents.
Top income shares in the US fell in steps with the world wars and the Depression, not smoothly with growth.
Policy (unions, minimum wages, progressive taxes) and the spread of schooling did much of the levelling, not violence alone.
Revolutionary violence expropriated the landlord class in a few years: levelling by force on a vast scale.
The Bolshevik project ended in forced collectivisation, which wiped out the better-off peasants and caused famine.
Across Seshat polities, military technology (iron, then cavalry) predicts jumps in social scale better than any other tested factor.
The retracted paper claimed moralizing gods appeared only after societies passed about a million people, as in the Persian empire.
Watching, punishing gods let strangers trust each other and so let groups grow beyond kin; Achaemenid kings invoked Ahura Mazda as guarantor of truth.
A moralizing faith came first and an empire after: a counter-case to complexity-first.
Plague a decade earlier had cut rents and revenues; lords and crown pressed survivors harder for the ransoms and war taxes of the 1350s.
The lowest lead emissions after 900 BCE coincide with the Plague of Cyprian and the third-century crisis.
Civil war and invasion disrupted Iberian and Balkan mining districts; the ice shows a nadir in emissions.
Defeat in France (Normandy lost 1450, Gascony 1453) discredited Henry VI and sent armed retainers and frustrated lords home.
The civil wars proved Parliament could beat the crown in the field; in 1688 the elites settled who controlled taxes and the army without another war.
